subject: history
promptStrong: Give me an exam-style {board} {level} {subject} question on {lo}, then mark my answer against the mark scheme.
promptWeak: Explain {lo} for {board} {level} {subject} simply, with a clear example and the most common mistake students make.

questions.q: In which year did Elizabeth I become Queen of England?
questions.explain: Elizabeth succeeded her half-sister Mary I in November 1558.

questions.q: Under the 1559 Act of Supremacy, what title did Elizabeth take over the Church of England?
options: Supreme Head of the Church of England
Supreme Governor of the Church of England
Defender of the Faith
Archbishop of Canterbury
questions.explain: Elizabeth was made Supreme Governor rather than Supreme Head of the Church of England.

questions.q: Which 1559 Act made the Protestant Book of Common Prayer compulsory and required people to attend church?
options: Act of Supremacy
Act of Uniformity
Act of Settlement
Act of Six Articles
questions.explain: The Act of Uniformity imposed the Book of Common Prayer and set fines for non-attendance.

questions.q: Who was Elizabeth's leading minister and Secretary of State, later created Lord Burghley?
options: Francis Walsingham
Robert Dudley
William Cecil
Thomas Cromwell
questions.explain: William Cecil (Lord Burghley) was Elizabeth's most trusted adviser for much of her reign.

questions.q: Why did Elizabeth adopt the title 'Supreme Governor' rather than 'Supreme Head' of the Church?
options: To avoid offending Catholics and those who objected to a woman being 'head' of the Church
Because Parliament refused to grant her any church authority
Because the Pope insisted on the change
Because she had not yet been crowned
questions.explain: The softer title was part of Elizabeth's attempt to avoid alienating Catholic and moderate opinion.

questions.q: Why is Elizabeth's 1559 Religious Settlement often described as a 'middle way' (via media)?
options: It abolished the Church of England entirely
It combined Catholic and Protestant elements to satisfy as many people as possible
It made England fully Catholic again
It banned all church services
questions.explain: The settlement kept some traditional practices while establishing a Protestant Church, aiming for broad acceptance.

questions.q: What was meant by a 'recusant' in Elizabethan England?
options: A person who refused to attend Church of England services
A Puritan preacher
A member of the Privy Council
A Spanish ambassador
questions.explain: Recusants, often Catholics, were fined for refusing to attend the official church.

questions.q: In which year was Mary, Queen of Scots executed?
questions.explain: Mary was executed at Fotheringhay Castle in February 1587 after the Babington Plot.

questions.q: In which year did the Spanish Armada attempt to invade England?
questions.explain: Philip II's Armada sailed against England in 1588 and was defeated.

questions.q: Who commanded the Spanish Armada in 1588?
options: Duke of Medina Sidonia
Duke of Parma
King Philip II
Duke of Alba
questions.explain: The Duke of Medina Sidonia led the Armada, while the Duke of Parma's army waited in the Netherlands.

questions.q: Why did the 1570 Papal Bull excommunicating Elizabeth increase the Catholic threat?
options: It ordered Catholics to attend Protestant services
It released English Catholics from obedience to Elizabeth and encouraged them to depose her
It made Elizabeth head of the Catholic Church
It banned Catholicism in Spain
questions.explain: The Bull 'Regnans in Excelsis' declared Elizabeth deposed, making loyal Catholics appear potential traitors.

questions.q: What was the main effect of the English fireships sent into Calais during the Armada campaign?
options: They sank most of the Spanish galleons
They forced the Spanish fleet to scatter and break its defensive crescent formation
They captured the Duke of Medina Sidonia
They blockaded the port of Cadiz
questions.explain: Panicked Spanish ships cut their anchors and scattered, exposing them to attack at Gravelines.

questions.q: What was the main aim of the Revolt of the Northern Earls in 1569?
options: To make Elizabeth Supreme Head of the Church
To replace Elizabeth with Mary, Queen of Scots and restore Catholicism
To unite England and Scotland peacefully
To support Protestant reform
questions.explain: The Catholic earls hoped to overthrow Elizabeth and put Mary on the throne.

questions.q: Elizabeth signed the 1585 Treaty of Nonsuch, sending troops under the Earl of Leicester to aid Dutch rebels. Why would this worsen relations with Spain?
options: It gave Spanish territory to France
It meant England was openly supporting Philip II's rebellious subjects in the Netherlands
It ended all English overseas trade
It required Elizabeth to become a Catholic
questions.explain: Open English intervention against Spanish rule in the Netherlands pushed the two countries towards war.

questions.q: During the Babington Plot, why was Walsingham able to secure the execution of Mary, Queen of Scots?
options: Mary publicly confessed to Parliament
His agents intercepted and decoded letters proving Mary had approved the plot to kill Elizabeth
The Pope handed over written evidence against Mary
Mary was captured leading an army into England
questions.explain: The decoded correspondence gave the evidence needed to try and execute Mary for treason.

questions.q: Which London playhouse, opened in 1599, is most closely associated with William Shakespeare's plays?
options: The Rose
The Theatre
The Globe
The Swan
questions.explain: The Globe opened in 1599 and was the home of Shakespeare's company, the Lord Chamberlain's Men.

questions.q: Why were 'sturdy beggars' (vagabonds) often punished harshly rather than helped?
options: They were seen as able-bodied people who chose not to work
They were all suspected of being foreign spies
They were wealthy landowners avoiding taxes
They were members of the clergy
questions.explain: The able-bodied 'undeserving' poor were viewed as idle and were punished, unlike the 'deserving' poor.

questions.q: Why did Puritans and some city authorities object to the theatres?
options: They believed theatres were too costly to build
They saw them as immoral and as sources of crime, disorder and disease
They wanted only Latin plays performed
They thought actors were paid too little
questions.explain: Critics linked playhouses to sin, crowds, crime and the spread of plague.

questions.q: An Elizabethan parish official meets an elderly man who is too ill to work and has no income. How would he most likely be classified and treated?
options: As one of the 'deserving' (impotent) poor, eligible for local relief
As a sturdy beggar to be whipped
As a recusant to be fined
As a vagabond to be executed
questions.explain: The old, sick and disabled were seen as the 'deserving' poor and given help by the parish.

questions.q: An English sailor returns from a colonising voyage to Virginia carrying tobacco and potatoes. Which explorer's expeditions are these most associated with?
options: Francis Drake
John Hawkins
Walter Raleigh
Martin Frobisher
questions.explain: Sir Walter Raleigh sponsored the Roanoke/Virginia voyages linked with the introduction of tobacco and potatoes.

specSource: Eduqas GCSE History specification; The Elizabethan Age 1558-1603
